learn.title: Pumped Hydro Storage: Earth's Biggest Battery
learn.intro: Pumped hydro storage is the world's largest battery technology, storing excess renewable energy by pumping water uphill during low demand and releasing it to generate electricity when needed. It provides critical grid stability and long-duration storage for a sustainable energy future.
learn.c1_text: Pumped hydro uses two water reservoirs at different elevations. During surplus energy, pumps push water uphill. When demand peaks, water flows down through turbines to generate electricity. Like a gravity-powered battery, it stores energy as potential water height.
learn.c2_text: Global pumped hydro capacity exceeds 1,600 GWh, supplying 90% of grid-scale storage. Round-trip efficiency is 70-85%, outperforming lithium-ion in longevity. Sites like China's Three Gorges Dam store 22.5 GWh, equivalent to 150,000 homes' daily power.
learn.c3_text: India plans 15 GW pumped hydro projects by 2030, including the 3,000 MW Nandikotkur project in Telangana. MNRE prioritizes these for renewable integration, leveraging Himalayan terrain to store surplus solar/wind energy and stabilize grids in states like Himachal Pradesh.
learn.stat2: China's Three Gorges Dam: 22.5 GWh storage
learn.stat3: India's target: 15 GW pumped hydro by 2030

learn.title: Grid Balancing: Real-Time Supply-Demand Match
learn.intro: The electricity grid dynamically balances supply and demand every second, preventing blackouts and ensuring reliable power. This real-time coordination integrates renewables, manages fluctuations, and maintains grid stability for homes, industries, and future energy needs.
learn.c1_text: Grid operators adjust generation to match demand within 10 seconds. If supply dips, reserves like spinning turbines instantly ramp up. Like a conductor, they synchronize power plants, using sensors to maintain 50/60 Hz frequency across interconnected grids worldwide.
learn.c2_text: Solar/wind farms use smart inverters to absorb excess energy as reactive power. Demand response programs incentivize consumers to shift usage during peaks. AI algorithms predict demand surges, enabling flexible resources like batteries to balance variability from renewables.
learn.c3_text: India's R-India project deploys IoT sensors and AI to balance its 300+ GW grid. State utilities use real-time data from 1.3 billion consumers. The Green Energy Corridor project transmits renewable power efficiently, supporting 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.

learn.title: Building-Integrated Photovoltaics: Solar Architecture
learn.intro: Building-Integrated Photovoltaics (BIPV) transforms solar panels into architectural elements like roofs, facades, and windows, merging clean energy generation with building design. This innovation reduces costs, enhances aesthetics, and accelerates renewable adoption in urban areas.
learn.c1_text: BIPV uses solar tiles, glass panels, or roofing shingles replacing traditional materials. Solar windows generate power while allowing light in. Like solar bricks, these integrate seamlessly into structures. Efficiency ranges 15-22%, with 30% of new EU buildings mandated to use BIPV since 2020.
learn.c2_text: BIPV eliminates separate racking and installation costs, offering 10-15% savings over traditional panels. Windows achieve 10-15% efficiency, while roof tiles match standard panels. Buildings generate 30-50% of their energy needs, reducing grid dependence and carbon footprints significantly.
learn.c3_text: India's SURE scheme mandates 20% BIPV in new government buildings. Projects like the 1.2 MW rooftop at Delhi's Oberoi Amarvilla hotel integrate solar glass. States like Gujarat offer subsidies for BIPV in industrial zones, targeting 100 GW solar by 2022 with 40% distributed generation.
learn.stat1: EU mandate: 30% BIPV in new buildings (2020)
learn.stat2: BIPV efficiency: 15-22% for tiles, 10-15% for windows
learn.stat3: India's SURE scheme: 20% BIPV in govt buildings
learn.stat4: BIPV cost savings: 10-15% vs traditional panels

learn.title: Electric Trucks & Buses: Zero-Emission Transport
learn.intro: Electric buses and trucks are revolutionizing commercial transport, cutting emissions and fuel costs. With advancing battery tech and charging infrastructure, these vehicles are becoming viable for urban transit and freight, driving sustainable mobility across India and globally.
learn.c1_text: Electric buses use lithium-ion batteries (250-350 kWh) for 200-300 km daily routes. Trucks achieve 400-800 km with solid-state batteries. Fast charging at depots takes 30-60 minutes. Like smartphones, they need efficient charging networks to replace diesel fleets entirely.
learn.c2_text: EVs reduce operating costs by 30-50% (fuel + maintenance). India's 10,000 electric buses save 1.5 million tons CO2 annually. Charging at night uses excess renewable energy. Lifecycle emissions are 60% lower than diesel, with 30% recyclable battery materials supporting circular economies.
learn.c3_text: India's FAME II scheme subsidizes 30% of EV bus costs, targeting 30,000 electric buses by 2030. Cities like Delhi operate 600+ electric buses. Tata Motors' Zip Electric truck serves 500+ fleet operators. State policies offer tax breaks for charging infra, aiming for 30% EV commercial vehicles by 2030.
learn.stat4: FAME II subsidy: 30% of EV purchase cost

learn.title: Rooftop Solar & Net Metering in India
learn.intro: Rooftop solar harnesses sunlight for clean energy, with net metering policies enabling households and businesses to sell excess power back to the grid. India's solar push drives affordable installations, reducing electricity bills and supporting decentralized renewable growth nationwide.
learn.c1_text: Panels convert sunlight to DC power, inverted to AC for home use. Excess energy flows to the grid via net metering, earning credits. A 1 kW system generates 1,200 kWh/year, offsetting 150 kg CO2. Like a battery, it stores value in grid credits when not consuming.
learn.c2_text: Under MNRE rules, consumers export surplus power at the same tariff they pay. No meters track exports separately—billing uses net consumption. For example, using 500 kWh and exporting 300 kWh results in paying for 200 kWh. Surplus credits roll over for 1 year, incentivizing oversized systems.
learn.c3_text: India's rooftop solar reached 9.5 GW in 2023, with Maharashtra leading at 2.1 GW. MNRE's subsidized loans (2% interest) and open access rules boost adoption. States like Tamil Nadu offer 100% subsidy for 3 kW systems under KUSUM. Over 10 million rooftop systems are expected by 2030.
learn.stat3: MNRE subsidies: Up to 40% for residential systems
learn.stat4: KUSUM scheme: 100% subsidy for 3 kW systems

learn.title: Carbon Markets: Pricing Pollution Clean
learn.intro: Carbon markets incentivize clean energy by assigning monetary value to emissions reductions. Through cap-and-trade systems and carbon credits, they drive investment in renewables, energy efficiency, and innovation, making pollution costly and sustainability profitable globally.
learn.c1_text: A carbon credit equals 1 ton of CO2 reduced or avoided. Companies buy credits to offset emissions, funding projects like wind farms. For example, a cement plant buying 10,000 credits pays $15-50/ton to cover 10,000 tons of CO2. Like pollution permits, they create financial incentives for clean tech.
learn.c2_text: Regulated sectors receive emission allowances; exceeding limits requires buying credits or cutting output. The EU ETS caps 2,000 million tons annually, with prices at €80/ton in 2023. Companies trade allowances like commodities, driving 40% emissions cuts in Europe since 2005 through market mechanisms.
learn.c3_text: India's Perform, Achieve, Trade (PAT) scheme mandates energy savings for heavy industries, enabling credit trading. The proposed National Carbon Market aims to link with global markets by 2025. Renewable energy projects earn Verified Carbon Units (VCUs), with 100+ Indian VCUs sold internationally last year under Article 6 rules.
learn.stat3: India's PAT scheme: 11th cycle targets 20% savings
learn.stat4: Global carbon market: $2 trillion potential by 2030
